title: Tabletop Battles Reviews Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave
content:
Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave is the eighteenth mainline game in Nintendo’s tactical RPG series, returning to the same world as Three Houses, the 2019 release that has spawned endless discourse to the detriment of humanity’s spirit. In Fortune’s Weave, players customize their own representative character, named Eshmel, and then select one of four characters to take through their own unique storylines: Cai, Dietrich, Theodora, and Leda. While the majority of the game follows the same turn-based tactical RPG format that Fire Emblem is known for, Fortune’s Weave re-introduces dungeon exploration mechanics and exploratory elements that weave in more traditional “RPG” elements, bringing some new life to the series. But is it worth picking up, especially if you’ve never played Fire Emblem before?

Your choices matter! Kinda. Not really, at least here.

To be honest, that question was one I had to ask myself; when I was asked to pick up this review, it made me realize that I had not actually gone through Three Houses or Engage, primarily due to dealing with chronic illness and work, which are bad combos! I’d seen people play both of them, but when I fired up Fortune’s Weave, I realized that the Fire Emblem I “knew” was back on my beloved 3DS, and essentially was throwing myself into a game I was only sort of familiar with. I knew the general idea of what to expect, but I was immediately struck by just how big this game is; at the time of this review, I’m about 15 hours into the game so far, and it feels like I have barely scratched the surface of what Fortune’s Weave has in store for me. Considering this was also the first review I’ve written for the site and my introductory post here in general, I also had some concerns about whether or not I was the right person to even talk about the game, but I’m honestly glad I did throw myself into the game so that I could share my thoughts on it, because it’s made me fall back in love with the series and with games that ask you to invest your time, but make it easy to do so, as well.

If you’re not that familiar with Fire Emblem, then the core of the game is a tactical RPG, where you move characters on a grid based map during combat, interacting with enemies through various types of attacks or abilities, like spells, ranged attacks, or other skills. Your characters can also support one another, and the general flow of combat works off of a rock-paper-scissors style triangle in regards to weaknesses or strengths for various attacks. This part was familiar to me and I was thankful for the fact that I knew what to do here, but the game is pretty hand-holdy when it comes to introducing you to how everything works; I think a very new player would find it very easy to pick up and learn the game’s flow from that.

Y'all, I went to that cave and beat the pants off of the things inside of it.

The rest of the game, though, was not exactly what I was expecting, and yet a lot of it felt oddly familiar. The overworld map is a sprawling top-down map that you can move your character through, with each step taking a unit of time from a set length of time you have until the next major event in the story. On the map you can find various nodes to interact with, shops, battles, and dungeons. This felt very boardgame-y to me, having to manage my time and travel as well as finding new events or encounters on the map as I explored. The dungeons were the most unexpected wrinkle, since the last time I saw this was back on the Gamecube (Remember that? Oh no, I’m old…), and they add a nice active wrinkle to the combat by changing up how your characters fight and interact. The dungeons are certainly not a major attraction but they are certainly fun and kind of interesting, and as I mentioned before, the game has a few accessibility tools to help newer players who may not be that familiar with RPGs. When you’re exploring dungeons, for example, you can turn on this tracker that shows you where you’ve come from and where you haven’t gone. I can understand the point of the tool, but it also reminds me of the Family Circus comic strip gag about foot prints, because it tracks everything you do and everywhere you go, which can look kind of overwhelming if you’re the type of player I am, which is to say a person who has to explore literally every single inch of a game! While you’re travelling, you can also engage in a Feast mechanic, which I find easiest to compare to the camping mechanic from Pokémon Sword & Shield. You select the Feast, pick what food ingredients you want to use, and your party will recover HP as well as other things, and can even deepen their bonds between one another while Feasting. I love when my Pokémon, I mean, soldiers, are all fed and happy!

I am sad to report you can NOT pet the cats. 0/10.

When you aren’t travelling the world map, you’ll probably spend most of your time in the city, which is a pretty shockingly huge 3D map to explore on foot. This place drives me crazy, primarily because I have to pick up everything I see in a game, and when the weekly timer resets, apparently so do most of the items. I’ve spent so much time running around this city clearing it of items only to see them come back that I had to stop and consider if I needed to continue picking them up (yes); there are a lot of characters to talk to, and to pursue various support conversations, you also need to know when and where characters will appear, as the time of day can affect your ability to interact with them. You can also find cats, which meow, but cannot be pet, I am sad to report.

Leda was my first choice, cause I love dancers and girlbosses.

Perhaps because I’m so used to the older Fire Emblem games, but I have to admit that I found Fortune’s Weave sort of daunting at first in size and scope; it just feels like there is so much to do and see in the game that it will take quite a while to get through every scenario and see everything the game has to offer. For my first playthrough I opted to play Leda, because I love an attractive lady who wants to girlboss her way through bloody revenge, and so far I have not been disappointed in her delivering exactly that. The protagonist that you pick at the start really doesn’t seem to have as much interaction with the game as I expected; unlike, say, Robin from previous games, I haven’t really seen “me” that much, instead playing through Leda. That may change further down the line, but it was something I noticed that felt a little different from previous iterations of the game.

Did I also mention she's hardcore?

The graphics and music are pretty great, with the usual Fire Emblem jingles and themes coming through along with various other new tracks set to the Mediterranean vibes that Fortune’s Weave is going for. I will say that the character models look great, but the backgrounds often look a little… less great. The city is huge, but it also looks a little flat, and the battle backgrounds also have “you are in a video game” vibe that sort of sucks out immersion while you watch the characters fight, which is a little bit of a bummer; the story is also fairly solid, and I’ve liked all of the character interactions and the main plot so far, and has certainly made me curious to see what the other protagonists offer once I’m done with Leda’s story.

Remember to take your Pokémon, er, soldiers, camping, I mean feasting, on curry, I mean--

I think that Fortune’s Weave is a great game, but far bigger than I had initially expected it to be. If you're looking for a game to sink maybe 100 hours or more into in order to see everything it has to offer, then Fortune’s Weave is absolutely the game you’ll want to pick up on your Switch 2. If you aren’t looking for that sort of commitment and investment though, I’d have to admit that the scope of the game will likely be a deterrent. For me, I’ve had a pretty long drought of games that have sucked me in for such an immense time, and I’ve really been enjoying what I’ve played so far. Primarily, I’ve been playing Dark Souls Remastered for the first time, or spending time on Dead by Daylight with friends, so Fortune’s Weave has sort of graciously fallen into my lap to fill a void I didn’t realize I had at the moment.

I'm pretty excited to see the rest of the Flame Lords once I've finished Leda's storyline. Also, girl, your hair is wild.

If you’re not that familiar with Fire Emblem games, I think Fortune’s Weave is a great starting point if you’re curious, since it has so much to offer and doesn’t make the game hard to get into. Once the main systems are explained, it can be fairly easy to continue playing and getting invested in the story of Eshmel and the city of Dagsion, as well as the characters you encounter and recruit. If you’re on the fence because you don’t tend to enjoy JRPGs, I think I’d give Fire Emblem a cautious recommendation, if only because the Switch 2 is a pretty hefty investment to begin with, and then the game itself is 70 dollars, so if you don’t think turn-based combat, character development and map management sound like something you’d enjoy, I’m not sure Fortune’s Weave is going to be the game that will change your mind. For myself, though, I’m having a blast, and I think once I do make my way through everything the game has to offer, I’ll finally go back and try Three Houses and Engage… the discourse over both games should have died down enough to have fun with them by now, right…?

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

title: The 7 best MTG cards in Multiverse Reforged
content:
The Jace Commander deck, or 'Multiverse Reforged' to give it its proper title, is a bit of a glorious mess. But while it might not play wonderfully out of the box and will never find its way onto our list of the best precons, that doesn't mean it isn't full of strong MTG cards.

In particular, Multiverse Reforged is stacked with some enormous, terrifying beaters and some clever new takes on legendary creatures. And a lot of them are more fun in the 99 of other decks than as commanders in their own right. Check out the best Multiverse Reforged cards below.

7. Darksteel Angel

One of the earliest cards revealed for the precon and easily up there with its greatest hits, Darksteel Angel is a more costly take on Platinum Angel, stopping opponents from winning the game while it's out on the field. You can go to -100 life, but as long as you have a Darksteel Angel, you're not out of the fight.

For the extra mana, you get some good value, though the stats haven't changed. For instance, this angel is indestructible, taking out a large swathe of cards that would normally be able to deal with it. It also blocks -1/-1 counters across your whole board, which will surely enable some horrid combo shenanigans with persist.

6. Venser, Fervent Forager

So, as Rachel Weeks from The Command Zone pointed out, if an opponent uses a clone card on your Venser, they can make two more copies of him, then use this to loop and create infinite hasty copies of everything on the board. So that's a pretty big downside.

Luckily, Venser makes for a fantastic finisher as soon as you play him. It's amazing at stealing your opponents' win conditions and doubling them. Whether it's for you or for your opponent, this guy wins games of Magic.

5. Ob Nixilis the Ascended

Is Ob Nixilis better as an angel than he ever was as a demon? Everyone loves a one-sided board wipe, and with this angel in your command zone, your opponents will have to think very carefully about how they commit to combat. If you use goading or tapping effects you can make him especially punishing.

Once Ob Nix makes it onto the battlefield, he's far from done being useful. With soul sister cards gaining you life on everyone's turns, it's pretty trivial to gain an extra 16/16 in flying stats every turn cycle.

4. Dack Fayden, Helping Hand

You get a creature! And you get a creature! Everybody gets a creature! This is a really funny concept for a commander, cheating goaded creatures into play for your opponents - while you get their ETBs. It seems like this would be best as a 'secret commander' in a different deck, just to give you a less restrictive color identity, but I think however you use Dack he's going to be heaps of fun and deceptively strong.

3. Memnarch, The Warden

Memnarch requires big ramp and colorless cost reducers to be playable, but he's well worth the effort and look at him - he knows it! While Menarch doesn't end games on the spot, he's very hard to get rid of, and will draw you a bazillion cards in an artifact deck. Underestimate him at your peril!

2. Niv-Mizzet, Ghost Counsel

Somehow, WotC made a Niv-Mizzet that is still doing almost exactly the same thing while still fitting a totally different color identity. It's nice that the Orzhov players get a chance to combo off with infinite card draw. This card is just plain cool and now I want to see a Simic and a Gruul Niv.

1. Avacyn, Angel of Horror

True to her name, evil Avacyn is scary-scary. While she might look worse than the original at first, the balance tips the other way if you assume you're playing this card alongside sacrifice outlets. Now she and everything else you control is almost impossible to get rid of and you're draining the hell out of everyone with Blood Artist.

title: Warhammer 40k 11th ed is only three months old, but the Space Marine codex is basically a new edition
content:
Since influencers with early copies of the upcoming Warhammer 40k 11th edition Space Marine codex and Munitorum Field Manual began to disclose the points costs for units, the community has been abuzz with discussions of just how busted this new force is going to be. Games Workshop had already warned us of a big upgrade to the Marines' stats, and now it seems they're only paying a minor points premium for the privilege. The changes will also ripple through a huge chunk of other armies that field variants of Space Marines - in terms of how the game feels to play, this looks like the end of Warhammer 40k 11th edition as we know it. And it's only been out for three months!

Every new Warhammer 40k Codex release, each balance dataslate, and each organised play pack represents a different meta for competitive Warhammer 40k players, but this is less subtle, and will reach into most forms of casual play - similar in scale, if not type, to the early errata to Warhammer 40k 10th edition needed to fix Titanic units and mortal wounds spam.

As well as the total overhaul to vanilla codex Space Marines, Games Workshop has confirmed that there will be digital updates to Dark Angels, Blood Angels, Space Wolves, Deathwatch, Black Templars, Grey Knights, Chaos Space Marines, Death Guard, Thousand Sons, Emperors Children, and World Eaters.

Depending on whether you count the five codex-compliant Space Marine chapters as separate armies, that's between one third and one half of all the Warhammer 40k factions. Until the codex is in the wild it is an open question whether these updated armies will be balanced between one another and against the rest of the game.

There has been somewhat reassuring news that the most egregious outliers won't be quite so cheap when the codex actually releases. Podcast La Voz de Horus reports it's had an update from GW about the points for Lion El'Jonson, which were initially insanely low but are now merely very, very affordable.

But even if the balance is spot on, this still represents a step change in how the game feels to play. Many armies will become more survivable, faster, better able to focus force, and worse at blanketing the board with bodies. Even assuming GW achieves those goals elegantly and with good game balance, why is this happening three months into a new edition, and not at the start?

Players who joined the game during 10th edition and stuck around have just experienced their first edition change. They've had to rethink their armies and strategies, and potentially grab some new model kits to adapt to the new game feel. Now the meta is going to shift again. For new players who started with 11th edition, all the experienced players at their store are muttering about massive changes to a system they're just beginning to get comfortable with.

I wonder if at one point the Warhammer 40k design team planned to launch 11th edition with these changes, maybe even with free Index rules for every army as we got with 8th and 10th edition. Smaller Space Marine armies feel part and parcel of the design sensibility that has limited conga-line units and made screening more challenging. The Psychic Levels rules and the 'Hunter' weapons profiles that are appearing in the new codexes look like universal features that fit in the core rules, and somehow didn't make it into the book.

Whatever the reason, I hope GW is watching closely to see what impact this scale of change has so soon after the launch of an edition, and learns the right lessons. What do you think? Is your community feeling mutinous, or is everyone sanguine? You can find me in the Wargamer Discord community if you'd like to share your thoughts.

title: BattleTech Mech Overview: Whitworth
content:
Some questions echo down the centuries, posed again and again until their elusive answers pass into legend. How much wood could a woodchuck chuck if a woodchuck could chuck wood? The world may never know! We certainly won't find the answer to that puzzler today. Blake willing, however, we may at least answer a parallel riddle: How much worth would a Whitworth have if a Whitworth it had worth?

That's right, today we're taking a look at the 40-ton vending machine for missiles known as the Whitworth!

Whitworth. credit: porble

It's easy for a 'Mech to feel unappreciated when "Worthless" is one of its in-universe nicknames, but despite a host of flaws both in and out of the BattleTech universe, nevertheless the Whitworth has persisted through the centuries, from the Age of War to the modern era, even inspiring the (potentially-ComStar-funded) establishment of a company dedicated to nothing but spare parts and upgrade kits for the venerable chassis, "Whitworth Specialty Manufacturing"! Let's see how it holds up against the ol' TTB rating system!

Variants

These mechs have all been reviewed based on a standard F through S scale, which you can find described on our landing page here (along with all of our other ‘Mech reviews, the name of the box you can buy to get any of the mechs we have covered, and our general methodology).

Whitworth. Credit: Rockfish

WTH-0

This isn't actually the original Whitworth, but rather the Limited Edition Extra Warcrimes version built for the Amaris Dragoons, but it's nevertheless strongly representative of the short-range members of the Whitworth lineage: Pantherlike 4/6/4 movement profile, 93% armor coverage doing the best it can, SRM 6 in each side torso, energy weapon in each arm in place of a hand, third energy weapon in the head. The only thing that sets this apart from the earlier-in-universe WTH-1S is that the left arm weapon is a (sinister!) flamer rather than a third medium laser.

The tiny engine on this mech has at least one positive knock-on effect, with eight of its 14 single heat sinks visible on the crit chart. Given three sinks padding each side torso and two in the CT, this mech is a lot less likely to explode than you'd expect from a slow, ammo-dependent 40-tonner without CASE. The Whitworth's legs, too, while a liability in canon or when playing with quirks, are padded out by the jump jets, helping insulate a little against mobility crits.

When judged by points cost (a low, low 863 BV) against its own contemporaries (the Trebuchet 5S, Hunchback 4SP, and Javelin 10N), the WTH-0 looks a little better than I expected, but when the timeline opens up, the Howler 6, Javelin 12N, Ion Sparrow B, and the like really do make it into an obsolete joke. It's just paddling uphill pairing this movement profile and armor layout with 3/6/9 weapons.

Lynn's Rating: D+.

WTH-1

The poster-child Whitworth, the WTH-1 is the result of the Star League saying "Hey, our Whitworth pilots keep getting killed trying to get close enough to use their SRMs?" Ten heat sinks (still with two padding each side torso), three Medium Lasers, same everything-else as the -0 or the -1S, but the missile launchers swap for two LRM 10s, still with a ton of ammo each. Neutral firing the LRMs at a run, builds one heat firing the lasers at a run; don't shoot everything at once please. 982 BV.

I've historically thought about the WTH-1 as "the bad Trebuchet 5N," but on further reflection that isn't really fair. Yes, it has noticeably weaker LRMs, and yes, it has lower ground speed, but the JJs genuinely are useful for getting into a good fire support position, the armor outside the CT is actually better, it doesn't have an unprotected ammo bomb like the 5N does, the backup lasers are almost exactly the same, and it's 209 BV cheaper. I'd also say it compares favorably to the average Valkyrie. None of this necessarily makes it good... mechs dependent on unenhanced Inner Sphere LRMs for value are also paddling upstream... but it's cheap enough I'd say it at least achieves "not-bad"!

Lynn's Rating: C.

WTH-1H

Where walks a missile mech, a funny Marian variant covered in rocket launchers will follow.

This is exactly a 1S (the 0, but with three MLs, no flamer), but with the right torso SRM 6 and its accompanying ammo dropped for EIGHT Rocket Launcher 10s. This has a higher BV cost than the SRM, going up to 993, but I'm going to surprise myself by saying that it might be worth it. We're still just under 1k, the rocket launchers provide something approaching "stand-off capability" for a mech otherwise limited to 3/6/9 range, and there are some coherent firing patterns here. The 1H can fire off four of the RL 10s heat-neutrally at a run, and the three lasers plus the SRM build +1 at a run, so firing half the rockets, the other half of the rockets, and then all the close range weapons across three turns while closing distance seems... plausible. You're still not particularly likely to hit shit with the rocket launchers, but if your dice spike in the right direction it would be, as Liberty might say, "mad funny."

Lynn's Rating: C-???

WTH-1S

The actual original Whitworth in-universe, because BattleTech's alphanumeric codes make no sense, the 1S is exactly a WTH-0 except with a third ML it doesn't have the heat capacity to fire elegantly jacking its BV up to 917. By every metric other than availability, I'd rather have the 0.

Lynn's Rating: D.

Whitworth. Credit: Rockfish

WTH-2

A Helm Renaissance refit, the 2 here is one of the least ambitious upgrades I've ever seen, dropping both arm lasers for Artemis IV on both LRMs. A side-grade at best, this increases the damage output of the LRMs while cutting the 2's close-range output by two-thirds. This ends up being something of a "win-more" Whitworth; more valuable when things are going to plan and it can hold back at long range, but nearly useless in the face of shit hitting the fan. At 936 BV it might fit into a few lists the WTH-1 wouldn't, though?

Lynn's Rating: C-.

WTH-2A

This is the first Whitworth to use any form of weight-savings tech! It was introduced in 3068!

Took 'em a minute, eh?

The 2A has basically nothing at all to do with the 2, aside from the same ol' engine, JJs, and armor layout that all the Whitworths up to this point have sported. It swaps to an Endo-Steel frame, mounts up ten double heat sinks, maintains the traditional arm medium lasers but drops the head gun down to a small laser, mounts a quartet of Streak SRM 4s with a single ton of ammo in the CASE'd right torso, and carries a C3S. It builds +1 heat on a running alpha strike if all the Streaks fire. 1,055 BV.

This is still slow, short-ranged, and kinda squishy, but there's a serious amount of damage potential here, and delivering most of this payload accurately at a range of 9 hexes sounds like a pretty funny payoff for a C3 network.

Lynn's Rating: C, maybe C+ in a C3 net.

4th Deneb Light Cavalry Whitworth. Credit: Valk

WTH-2H

A weirdo RecGuide take on the OG Whitworth loadout, the 2H sticks with a Standard Engine but shifts to a higher rating, moving a sprightly-for-a-Whitworth 5/8/4. The arm lasers shift to ERMLs, while the head laser is still a regular ML. The missile launchers shift to lighter MRM 10s with Apollo FCS, with their two tons of ammo in the CASE II-protected left torso, and the armor shifts to Heavy Ferro-Fibrous... so it can maintain the exact same coverage as every other Whitworth up to this point. With ten doubles for heat sinks, this builds 1+ Movement heat on an alpha strike. 1,148 BV.

This is interesting. It would benefit from having a C3S like most of the other Jihad-or-later Whitworths, but the Core Rules MRM changes are good for it... firing Saturation Mode with 10-tube launchers is probably a fool's errand, but just the ability to use them as normal weapons without any special maluses is helpful. Even the mix of ER and regular lasers kinda makes sense here, not just for heat reasons, but in mirroring the MRM's range bands: the ERMLs hit the same 8-hex medium range, while the regular ML has the same 3-hex short range. I kinda wish it didn't have the short jump range, but they're only costing it about 90 BV and are still situationally handy.

At the end of the day I think the WTH-2H's biggest problem is that 5/8/4 is still slow for a 40-tonner, and that feels extremely fixable. While I do appreciate a SFE as a durability add, with an XL engine this same exact mech could go 7/11/0 with full armor and a C3S and the BV cost would only go to 1,199! That mech might excite me; as-is, the 2H seems usable, but perhaps a bigger jump in BV than its actual jump in capability would warrant.

Lynn's Rating: C.

WTH-3

This is the endo-steel skeleton of a 2A, but with ten single heat sinks, four LRM 5s with four tons of ammo, a C3S, and a full load of Improved Jump Jets taking its movement to 4/6/6. At 861 BV it's the BV-cheapest Whitworth.

This mech is badly impacted by the new Core Rules not allowing LRM 5s to deliver minefields or smoke. The four tons of ammo here are begging to be a toolbox, but a 50/50 mix of Narc-enabled and semi-guided is about the best you can manage.

"Cheap, mobile enough, and able to annoy people from range" kinda takes this into Liberty's "Little Bastard" zone, but I'm not particularly impressed, especially given that it's all-but-helpless against anything which won't allow it to stay at range.

Lynn's Rating: C-.

Lyran Commonwealth Whitworth. Credit: SRM

WTH-5S

Finally living up to the promise of "What The Hell," this experimental Lyran (provincial) variant, which never saw regular production, has a lot going on. It buys a good bit of tonnage by swapping to an XL engine without increasing its rating and also moving to Composite Structure (oof), then spends that mounting an MXPL and AES in each arm, Streak SRM 6s in each side torso (with one ton of ammo in a CASE II-protected bin), a Guardian ECM in the CT, and a Supercharger. It builds movement heat on an Alpha if both Streaks lock. It's the most BV-expensive Whitworth at 1,230.

This feels utterly cursed. MXPLs with AES are a good time, and I always like a good Streak launcher, but the Composite Structure is absolutely the wrong way to save weight, and the Supercharger is absolutely the wrong way to increase speed.

No, bad, no fancy tech toys for you, Supervising Technician Eric Stillman of the Spillman Provincial Refit Facility on Acrux!

Lynn's Rating: D--.

WTH-K

Another endo-steel variant like the 2A and the 3, the WTH-K scrapes the edge of greatness (or at least goodness) like a semi trailer scraping under a can-opener bridge. It has ERMLs for the arm lasers. C3S in the head. MML 7s in each side torso; two tons of ammo total don't give much wiggle room, but at least let it carry the basics. It curiously mounts five IJJs for a 4/6/5 movement profile, deeply weird, but it hits a TMM breakpoint, so it's not the worst.

I love MMLs, and even though the K lacks CASE, this seems like a good loadout! There's just one teeeeeeensy little problem.

This builds 18+Movement heat on an Alpha Strike, perfect for base load of Double Heat Sinks!

Naturally, of course, it mounts ten Singles instead!

There are perfectly fine firing patterns here, but they're a shadow of what might have been. Basically, the K is going to fire LRMs until it hits minimum range, then swap to the ERMLs, then swap to the SRMs when it hits three hexes. Sure, entirely rational bracket firing. Except the Whitworth could do better damage than that at SRM range back when it was using IntroTech!

This just makes my heart sad, such wasted potential. It is at least cheap at 958 BV, but I can't even call it best-in-class of C3-enabled 40-tonners with Standard Engines and double MMLs, not while the Battle Cobra BTL-C-2OE exists!

Lynn's Rating: D+.

Hastati Sentinels Whitworth. Credit: Jack Hunter

Final Thoughts

Wow. I really can't say I've seen another Spheroid mech that's been around for as long as the Whitworth which comes this close to being an OmniMech. The armor layout never changes. The engine almost never changes. The inner structure does, but outside the experimental 5S it only comes in Standard and IS Endo-Steel flavors. It never gives up jump jets completely. Very consistent, very mediocre, elevated to usability mainly because it's also very cheap.

I guess that's the final verdict: Whitworth, Worthless? No, Worth Less!

title: The best MTG Commanders 2026
content:
The Commander is the legendary creature that leads your other 99 cards into battle in games of EDH: they dictate the colors you can include in your deck, and shape your overall strategy. If you're shopping for new options, our tried-and-tested guide to the best MTG commanders recommends plenty that reliably secure wins and are extremely fun to play.

Wizards of the Coast introduces more legendary creatures with each year of new MTG sets, but this guide will help you keep up with the latest releases and meta shifts. If you want to get really competitive, you'll be better served by our dedicated cEDH tier list. Or, if you're just starting out with this format, we'd recommend starting out with MTG commander precon decks instead.

Top commanders MTG:

  • Atraxa, Praetors' Voice
  • Edgar Markov
  • Vivi Ornitier
  • Teval, the Balanced Scale
  • Baylen, the Haymaker
  • The Necrobloom
  • Kenrith, The Returned King
  • Muldrotha, The Gravetide
  • Tymna The Weaver
  • The Gitrog Monster
  • Isshin, Two Heavens As One
  • Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow
  • Sauron, The Dark Lord
  • The Ur Dragon
  • Kaalia Of The Vast
  • Lathril, Blade Of The Elves
  • Pantlaza, Sun Favored
  • Shroofus Sproutshire
  • Atraxa, Grand Unifier

Atraxa, Praetors' Voice

While not quite the dominant force she was in 2016, Atraxa, Praetors' Voice still makes for a top commander. Her proliferate ability opens up all kinds of avenues and has only gotten more flexible as Wizards experiments with new types of counters like shield and stun.

Atraxa is a really great commander to experiment with because her ability and color identity mean you can explore about six different themes. You could make a pretty standard +1/+1 counter deck, or go the opposite route with -1/-1 counters. You could be really unpleasant and run with poison counters, or create a superfriends deck full of planeswalkers.Whatever route you go, you're probably going to want more effects that proliferate, so cards like Ezuri, Stalker of Spheres and Tekuthal, Inquiry Dominus are a perfect fit. They also often lend themselves to a Phyrexian theme!

Game Changers for Atraxa, Praetor's Voice

  • Fierce Guardianship
  • Force of Will

Edgar Markov

The Commander 2017 set was all about tribal decks, each focused on a single creature type: cats, wizards, dragons, and vampires. Edgar Markov led the cats - no, sorry, the vampires deck - and quickly rose to the status of top commander. While the card got horribly pricey as a result, a reprint in Innistrad Remastered has made him a little less silly to buy.

With the ability to create a swarm of little nippers, then pump them up each time he attacks, Edgar naturally works best in a horde-style deck that can swiftly overwhelm opponents. Mardu colors give you access to all the top removal cards, and best of all, Edgar's eminence ability makes him useful from the command zone, where he can churn out mini-mes in safety.

You then need stuff to do with all your vampire tokens, like buffing them up or sacrificing them for card draw with Skullclamp and draining your opponent with Blood Artist.

Game Changers for Edgar Markov

  • Braids, Cabal Minion

Vivi Ornitier

MTG's Final Fantasy set was stuffed with legendary creatures, but Vivi Ornitier is the real standout for Commander players. He grows more powerful every time you cast a non-creature spell, and that power in turn fuels an incredibly versatile mana-making ability.

Vivi can be hard to keep in play due to his notoriety (he did terrible things in Standard) but on the bright side, his mana cost is so low that it shouldn't be too hard to bring him back. Keep him on the board long enough, and Vivi becomes a powerful attacker in his own right, but his real value lies in the win conditions you can create with the killer combination of free mana and pinging. A Curiosity-type card also makes this guy a card draw machine.

With Vivi, your game plan might be a spellslinger or storm build - setting up until the perfect turn allows you to combo off. Alternatively, you could go all in on pingers, and aim to whittle your opponents down with a million tiny cuts.

Game Changers for Vivi

  • Cyclonic Rift
  • Mystical Tutor
  • Rhystic Study

Teval, the Balanced Scale

Teval, the Balanced Scale offers fantastic value, especially for a precon commander. This spicy spirit dragon has seen its popularity soar since Tarkir: Dragonstorm, and no wonder. It's a consistent source of land and tokens whose self-mill strategies synergize with a variety of decks.

Obviously, a straightforward graveyard deck is the first place to go. You want cards entering and leaving your graveyard as often as possible to trigger Teval's ability. After that though, you could consider a lands-matter sub-theme, playing multiple lands a turn to stack up the triggers. You could look to get the most from your tokens with zombie tribal cards too.

Your biggest problem will be defending Teval, who has no protection against removal, will suffer when cards are exiled, and who must constantly jump into the fray of battle.

Gamechangers for Teval

  • Force of Will
  • Fierce Guardianship
  • Gifts Ungiven

Baylen, the Haymaker

If you love using tokens, Baylen, the Haymaker might just be the best commander in all of Magic: The Gathering history, but he has surprising depth - this isn't just your typical go-wide tokens leader.

You wouldn't necessarily know that from the first step of your gameplan though: you begin by amassing a token army. They don't all have to be creatures, you can use treasure or food as well. But after this step is where the rabbit is flexible.

If you want to win with commander damage, you can tap your tokens to buff Baylen up with counters and swing for lethal. He turns four tokens into three +1/+1 counters, so even without built-in protection, this is very doable.

Alternatively, you can use your tokens for mana and card draw. That lets you dig through your deck and cast other key pieces that will help you convert tokens into victory.

I'll lastly add that there are few better commanders to pick for an Hare Apparent deck, if you just want to overwhelm your foes with a lupine legion.

Gamechangers for Baylen

  • Smothering Tithe
  • Biorhythm
  • Aura Shards

The Necrobloom

The Necrobloom is easy for opponents to underestimate. On its early turns, it doesn't seem to achieve much - play a land, fetch a land, create a puny plant token. However, if left undisturbed for long enough, it's landfall antics will start to cause serious problems.

As soon as seven types of land are under your control, you can start building a zombie army, all while blocking with your chunky commander their numerous plant buddies. Dredge is on hand to bring back any crucial lands, and it opens up plenty of interactions that keep The Necrobloom's tokens-and-landfall schtick feeling interesting.

Mass land-reanimation is particularly deadly in this deck, creating a huge horde that has to be dealt with in one turn cycle, else it's game over.

Gamechangers for the Necrobloom

  • Field of the Dead
  • Crop Rotation

Kenrith, The Returned King

Five-color commanders are some of the strongest because they allow you to use any card in the game. That means ultimate flexibility. As a result, they're a little controversial, since many lend themselves to less focused strategies and decks, where you just want to cram in all the best cards in your collection.

But we think that's as valid a playstyle as any - and it's hard to pass up jack-of-all-trades commanders when they're as good as Kenrith, the Returned King. Kenrith shines because all of his abilities are useful, and some are invaluable. You only need white mana to cast him, so you can have him out on the field and gradually unlock new abilities as you play new lands.

He's a top commander for those still learning how to play Magic The Gathering's most popular format, since you can experiment to your heart's content, and it's hard to go too wrong. Synergy is not required - just brute strength!

Gamechangers for Kenrith

  • Coalition Victory
  • Gifts Ungiven
  • Fierce Guardianship

Muldrotha, The Gravetide

Do you hate it when your opponents blow up your stuff? Then Muldrotha, the Gravetide is the top commander for you. Allowing you to play one card of each permanent type from your graveyard each and every turn, this noxious elemental turns your graveyard into an extension of your hand.

Unfortunately, with a high cost and incredible ability, Muldrotha is one of those commanders that attracts removal like a magnet. On the bright side, her Sultai colors (black, green and blue) give you access to a ton of power outside of her own impressive strength, including excellent creatures, removal, and card draw.

And when you do manage to protect her for long enough to make good use of her resurrection powers, your opponents are going to have a bad time.

Gamechangers for Muldrotha

  • Gifts Ungiven
  • Intuition
  • Fierce Guardianship

Tymna The Weaver

Tymna the Weaver may not look like much from the outset - sure, she draws cards when you hit people, whatever. But never underestimate the power of friendship. Tymna is a top commander choice because she has the Partner ability, which - like Tymna herself - was introduced in the Commander 2016 set. That means you can pair her up with any legendary creature that also has 'Partner' to give them joint leadership of your commander deck.

Two commanders are better than one, since they unlock new card options and new synergies, as well as ensuring you always have a creature to play out. Tymna makes this list simply because she's one of the most versatile creatures with the Partner ability. The card draw she provides will be valuable, whatever strategy you're going for.

Tymna the Weave is most often paired up with the merfolk card Thrasios, Triton Hero. That's because this combination gives you access to four colors and two commanders with generically powerful abilities. They don't make Partners like this anymore, and for good reason.

Gamechangers for Tymna

  • Thassa's Oracle
  • Orcish Bowmasters

The Gitrog Monster

A froggy chap with a winning smile, The Gitrog Monster has a series of unique, versatile abilities that make for a powerful MTG commander. It lets you play more lands, allowing for copious ramping, and you get to draw cards each time you put lands in the graveyard.

Cards like Crucible of Worlds will help you bring valuable lands back to the battlefield so you can sacrifice them again and again for endless utility. Even a simple Evolving Wilds can be extremely useful for Gitrog.

Whether you're using discard outlets or sacrificing lands, there's plenty of ways to generate absurd value with this top commander. You can also abuse infinite combos, which makes The Gitrog Monster a viable combo deck in cEDH.

Gamechangers for the Gitrog Monster

  • Crop Rotation
  • Field of the Dead
  • Glacial Chasm

Isshin, Two Heavens As One

Isshin, Two Heavens as One has just one simple ability, but its elegance and simplicity belies its power. This high tech samurai doubles up all your attack triggers, letting you generate absurd value whenever you swing at your opponents.

Not the best commander for anyone who likes playing a slower, defensive game, Isshin wants you to strike hard and strike fast. While all Isshin decks want to attack, this is another commander that you can build in a few ways, as there are loads of strong creature cards to choose from, and plenty of room for building up subthemes.

Even better, his very affordable mana cost means you don't have to worry too much about removal spells, as you can play Isshin, Two Heavens as One several times without it becoming too taxing.

Gamechangers for Isshin

  • The One Ring
  • Jeska's Will
  • Teferi's Protection

Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow

If you like ninjas, then Magic: The Gathering has a brilliant commander option. With Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow, your whole deal is striking with low-cost, evasive creatures, then launching your commander into play with ninjitsu, and reaping the rewards: plenty of card draw, and plenty of pain.

The best thing about Yuriko is, as long as you have an unblocked creature, you can always get her into play for two mana. This is huge. It means no matter how many times your opponents deal with your commander, it's always a threat.

The rest of your deck is not so resilient to a board wipe - and a board wipe can seriously set you back, though you can usually hold up a counterspell or two to protect your ninja army. Yuriko makes for a top budget commander deck too - little unblockable guys don't tend to cost too much.

Gamechangers for a Yuriko deck

  • Force of Will
  • Consecrated Sphinx
  • Cyclonic Rift

Sauron, The Dark Lord

A six-cost commander in Grixis, a color combo not exactly known for ramp, is a tough sell. However, if you can hang on and play Sauron, the Dark Lord, you're all set to have a great time. He's a self-fueling engine.

Once Sauron comes down, he starts to roll an unstoppable boulder at your opponent. No one wants to pay the ward cost to get rid of him, and every time anyone casts a spell, you get another Amass trigger.

Soon, your Orcs will be enormous, something on your board will be very hard to block, and you'll be drawing several cards a turn. Sauron works great with several cards from the Lord of the Rings set, which have a very high power level. And you can bring in all the old Amass cards from War of the Spark, too.

He can also reliably pitch your hand into your graveyard, which can make a good setup for graveyard strategies - whether you're trying to get an Underworld Breach / Lion's Eye Diamond loop going for a combo, or just want to reanimate something huge.

Gamechangers for a Sauron deck

  • Demonic Tutor
  • Lion's Eye Diamond
  • Underworld Breach

The Ur Dragon

The Ur Dragon offers a simple strategy, but it's still powerful enough to stampede casual commander tables (and steal a few more competitive wins, too). Its Eminence keyword means that, whether this card is on the battlefield or not, all your MTG dragons are one mana cheaper. The plan should be clear from here - fill your deck with huge, hard-hitting fliers and let rip.

The Ur Dragon is very expensive to get on the battlefield. However, it's a 10/10 flyer that allows you to draw cards equal to the number of your attacking dragons. Even better, you can then place a permanent from your hand onto the battlefield for free.

There are plenty of cards that synergize with The Ur Dragon's matter-of-fact battle plan. Prioritize those that give you extra benefits for playing dragons onto the battlefield or that can make these mana-hungry creatures even cheaper. You'll also need a solid ramp plan if you want your enormous dragons to get off the ground.

Gamechangers for The Ur Dragon

  • Mana Vault
  • Ancient Tomb
  • Chrome Mox

Kaalia Of The Vast

Kaalia of the Vast has been considered a top commander almost since the format's inception. Even today, this card's powers are impressive. Kaalia is a four-cost Mardu commander with flying and the ability to add a card from your hand to the battlefield whenever she attacks. That card must be an Angel, Demon, or Dragon creature, and it's automatically tapped and attacking along with Kaalia.

This is a ferociously fast way to cheat flying threats onto the field. If you can give Kaalia haste, your chosen commander can start handing out freebies as early as turn four. Lightning Greaves, Swiftwood Boots, and Dragon Tempest are your friend here.

Naturally, you'll want a deck full of angels, demons, and dragons to back Kaalia up. You should also leave space for problem-solving cards. Kaalia is a veteran of the competitive commander scene, so you can expect many players to have a game plan when she shows up - removal, removal, and removal.

Gamechangers for a Kaalia of the Vast deck

  • Teferi's Protection
  • Demonic Tutor
  • Imperial Seal


Lathril, Blade Of The Elves

As one of the oldest and best-established creature types in all of Magic: The Gathering, elves have long been a super powerful tribe. There's just been so much time for Wizards to print good elves, and there are now so many of them standing around pouting and hugging trees that it's almost too easy to make a strong elves deck. Just find the cards with the pointy ears and chuck a bunch in.

Lathril, Blade of the Elves is a Kaldheim commander who provides a nice bit of edge for elves decks by adding black to their color identity. This top commander also gives you a powerful new win condition, letting you use your elvish army to drain your opponents for huge chunks of life.

Lathril gives you plenty of options. You can build her to be a classic green elves deck, which ramps up quickly to a critical mass of creatures and then pulls out one of umpteen win conditions. But you can also create a combo style deck that relies on untappers to build up infinite mana, or uses them with Lathril herself to close out the game.

Gamechangers for Lathril

  • Natural Order
  • Survival of the Fittest
  • Gaea's Cradle

Pantlaza, Sun-Favored

Open the door, get on the floor, and prepare to walk the dinosaur, with one of the most popular MTG commanders of recent years. There's a good reason Pantlaza Sun-Favored sees so much play. Coming out of one of the best precon decks ever released, this raptor is a top commander choice if you just want to throw around some big stompy dinosaurs.

Pantlaza's Discover ability means that each dinosaur you cast has the potential to trigger a cascade, letting you fetch up one or potentially more other random dinosaurs from your deck (worst case scenario you hit a mana rock or something). It feels great to start a turn with just your commander on board, and end it with a herd of colossal reptiles whose approaching roars tell your opponents that you are very much the threat. Just make sure you pack enough ramp!

The randomness of this ability might be frustrating to some, but for others it'll ensure their deck always feels fresh.

Gamechangers for Pantlaza

  • Teferi's Protection
  • Farewell
  • Gaea's Cradle

Shroofus Sproutsire

We're not sure if Shroofus Sproutsire truly deserves to be on a list of all-time top commanders, but we've included him as an added extra because we couldn't bear to upset the lil' guy. He's certainly one of the best Jumpstart 2025 Commanders at any rate.

You're always going to have to put a bit of work in to land a hit with this commander, but once you get the ball rolling it's going to move very very fast. While he'd probably work better as Slimefoot's right hand man, this creature will feel like having Scute Swarm in your command zone.

Gamechangers for Shroofus Sproutshire

  • Gaea's Cradle
  • Natural Order
  • Seedborn Muse

Atraxa, Grand Unifier

Alright, Atraxa, Grand Unifier comes with an eye-watering mana cost, and it doesn't have the explosive proliferate powers of our other favored Atraxa commander. However, Grand Unifier offers heaps of power and versatility.

This is a mighty 7/7 commander with flying, vigilance, deathtouch, and lifelink. If you can keep Atraxa in play, it'll obliterate opposing forces, dole out enormous chunks of commander damage, and keep you well-defended in the meantime.

Perhaps more important is Atraxa's enters-the-battlefield ability. This allows you to reveal ten cards from the top of your library. For each card type among those, you can put one card of each revealed type into your hand. The rest go on the bottom of your library in a random order.

This is a commander with fairly generic powers that can feel a bit 'jack of all trades, master of none'. However, this also makes Atraxa suitable for a variety of deck types, from Blink to Phyrexian Typal.

Gamechangers for Atraxa, Grand Unifier

  • Thassa's Oracle

title: [40k] Ruleshammer 11th Edition: Transports (Updated September 23, 2026)
content:
Welcome back to Ruleshammer! In this series we take a detailed look at the rules of key games, but Warhammer 40k in particular. This week I’m looking at Transports in 11th edition!

Changelog

  • Update (Latest): 2026-09-23 Added section on Assault and Shock Disembark moves.
  • Published: 2026-07-24

Transport Capacity

Every model has a specific set of criteria regarding which models it can carry and how many of them, not that this limit is purely a max model count though Transports can contain more than one unit.

TRANSPORT models have a transport capacity listed on their datasheet. This determines the type and maximum number of friendly models that are eligible to embark within them. More than one unit can be embarked within the same TRANSPORT model at the same time, provided it has sufficient transport capacity.

Some of these transport rules can be quite specific and will vary between different transports in your army. For instance Rhinos and Impulsors differ in specific models they can transport. The Rhinos:

RHINO TRANSPORT RULE: This model has a transport capacity of 12 ADEPTUS ASTARTES INFANTRY models. It cannot transport JUMP PACK, WULFEN, PHOBOS, GRAVIS, CENTURION, TERMINATOR or TACTICUS models (excluding TACTICUS CHARACTER models that began the battle attached to a non-TACTICUS unit).

vs. the Impulsors:

IMPULSOR TRANSPORT RULE: This model has a transport capacity of 7 TACTICUS or PHOBOS INFANTRY models. It cannot transport JUMP PACK models.

For many armies there’s a distinct progression of transports capable of carrying larger and larger models; Space Marines, for instance, need a Land Raider before they can carry models as big as Terminators or Centurions.

LANDRAIDER TRANSPORT RULE: This model has a transport capacity of 12 ADEPTUS ASTARTES INFANTRY models. Each JUMP PACK, WULFEN, GRAVIS or TERMINATOR model takes up the space of 2 models and each CENTURION model takes up the space of 3 models.

Now that we know what models we can put in our transports, let's move on to using them in a game.

Before the Battle Begins

Players decide what units will be in which transports during the Mission sequence; it’s not something you’re locked into when you muster your army. You actually know a bit of information about the battle you’re about to fight before you have to make these decisions.

Before the battle, in the Declare Battle Formations step, your units can start embarked within any friendly TRANSPORT model that has sufficient transport capacity remaining for the whole unit.

The Declare Battle Formations step is fairly straight forward.

Players secretly note down in order:

    1. Which of their units will start the battle embarked within which TRANSPORTS.
    2. Which of their units will start the battle in Strategic reserves.

Be aware that if you do put a Transport into Strategic Reserves, both the Transport and the units embarked inside it count towards the 50% points limit for Strategic reserves.

Unless otherwise stated, the combined points value of all of your strategic reserves units (including those embarked within TRANSPORTS that are themselves placed in strategic reserves) cannot exceed 50% of your points limit for your battle size.

One aspect of this that players don’t have a choice in since the July 2026 update, though, is if their Dedicated Transports can begin the battle empty or not. Missing from the launch version of 11th edition, that requirement has been re-added to rule 18.01:

A friendly unit must be embarked within each friendly DEDICATED TRANSPORT model. At the end of this step, each friendly DEDICATED TRANSPORT model without an embarked unit is destroyed, but they do not trigger rules that are triggered when a model is destroyed.

So Dedicated Transport models like the Space Marine Rhino, the Leagues of Votann Sagitaur, or the T'au Devilfish MUST have a unit embarked inside of them at the start of the battle or they are destroyed.

Embarking

Embarking in transports requires a unit to have met a series of criteria and made some specific move types; it is not, however, limited to any single phase or even just the controlling player's turn. I’ll get back to this nuance in a moment.

Once the first battle round has started, a friendly unit can embark within a friendly TRANSPORT model after making a normal, advance or fall-back move, if all of the following conditions apply:

    • Each model in that unit is within 3" of that TRANSPORT.
    • That unit was not set up on the battlefield this turn.
    • That unit is eligible to embark within that TRANSPORT, as described on that TRANSPORT’s datasheet.
    • That TRANSPORT has sufficient remaining transport capacity for each model in that unit.

Most of these criteria are pretty obvious; that you can’t embark inside a transport that doesn’t have room for the whole unit shouldn’t come as a surprise. Some of the others, though, are a bit more nuanced.

Each model in that unit is within 3" of that TRANSPORT.

This criteria, for instance, has varied from edition to edition, but in 11th edition the requirement is that every model in the Unit must be within 3”. Here’s what that looks like.

That unit was not set up on the battlefield this turn.

Without some special ability your units can’t arrive on the battlefield and then embark in the same turn; remember that Disembarking counts are being set up on the battlefield, though! You can’t disembark from one transport and embark into another without a special rule saying your unit can do that or something similar, such as the Drukhai Aerialists rule that lets a unit embark at the end of the fight phase.

Take note, though, that this limit only applies to the turn, NOT the round. This is where the lack of a phase or turn limit comes into play. If you have some way of making a normal, advance, or fall-back move in your opponent's turn, units can use this move to embark.

In your opponent's Movement phase, if an enemy unit ends a move within 8" of this unit, if this unit is not within Engagement Range of one or more enemy units, this unit can make a Normal move of up to D6"

What Can Embarked Units do?

A short question with a fairly complex answer. The July 2026 update has added a number of clarifications for Embarked Units.

01.02.04 Not on the Battlefield

A unit that is embarked within a TRANSPORT or that is in strategic reserves is not on the battlefield. The following applies to such units.

    • That unit is NOT visible to any other units (units are visible to themselves).
    • Any other unit is NOT visible to that unit.
    • Players cannot measure distances to or from that unit (units are within range of their own abilities).

This means that units not on the battlefield cannot be selected or targeted by any attack or rule that requires a unit to be visible or within a certain distance (other than their own abilities).

Such units can still use their other rules, and are still units in the controlling players army and so can be affected by rules that require a player to select a unit from an army, as well as rules that affect all units in an army.

The control player must take battle-shock rolls for units that are not on the battlefield in their Command Phase if they are battle-shocked, or if they are below half strength.

It’s hard to really summarise this into any fewer words than it already is. Suffice it to say the important elements here are that you can use stratagems on embarked units, embarked units can still benefit from their own abilities, and embarking a unit doesn’t prevent you from needing to do Battle-shock tests.

So abilties like Abbadon's The Warmaster would still function, and allow the controlling player select an aura for him as usual, though the aura itself wouldn't benefit any other models as you can't measure distances to embarked units, so no unit can be within the aura. Abbadon would technically be within range of his own aura whilst embarked, but he doesn't actually have the keywords to be affected by it so that doesn't do anything.

Firing Deck, Leader Abilties and Enhancements

Firing Deck is much the same in 11th edition, though considerably more wordy about it.

This ability always takes the form Firing Deck X. In your Shooting phase, each time this TRANSPORT is selected to shoot, if one or more units are embarked within it, resolve the following sequence:

    1. Select up to X models embarked within this TRANSPORT (excluding models whose units have already been selected to shoot this phase).
    2. For each selected model, select one of its ranged weapons (excluding [ONE SHOT] weapons).
    3. Until this TRANSPORT has resolved all of its attacks, it has all of those selected weapons in addition to its other weapons.
    4. Until the end of the turn, units embarked within this TRANSPORT are not eligible to shoot.

The Transport gains the weapons of the embarked unit, and now you might wonder, if the units' abilities are working can Leader abilities and Enhancments affect these weapons that the Transport has gained. No. As of the July 2026 FAQ it's been ruled that only the attached unit benefits from leader abilities and enhancements, and the Transport isn't part of the attached unit.

Q: While an attached unit is embarked within a TRANSPORT, do weapons that TRANSPORT shoots with using the Firing Deck ability gain any benefit from any abilties that attached leader has (e.g. a Lieutenant's Tactical Precision ability that grants weapons in it's unit the [LETHAL HITS] ability?

A: No. Firing Deck enables a TRANSPORT to be equipped with a number of weapons equipped by it's passengers (Core Rules), bu the TRANSPORT itself is not part of that attached unit.

So whilst not ambiguous, I would forgive players for thinking that an enhancement or ability that changes those weapons would still have changed them when the Transport borrows them but alas not. For good measure this was FAQed again in August 2026 but doesn't change the result.

Q: Do a unit's abilities continue to function while they are embarked within a TRANSPORT?

A: Yes, within the restrictions specified by the ability itself. Embarked units are Not On The Battlefield (01.02.04), so any ability requiring visibility or measurement to another unit will fail. Example: Azrael is attached to an Intercessor Squad unit and embarked within a TRANSPORT, and that TRANSPORT is making a shooting attack using the Firing Deck ability. While Azrael's Supreme Grand Master ability is still technically active, it will have no effect, as the requirements of the ability are not met (the ability affects 'weapons equipped by models' in Azrael's unit, and for the purposes of Firing Deck, the TRANSPORT itself is equipped with those weapons instead).

Disembarking

Disembarking is perhaps the most codified it’s ever been in Warhammer 40k in this edition. There are now three distinct modes of Disembark you need to be aware of.

from Warhammer 40k 11th Edition Core Rules - Games Workshop

Rapid Disembark: This mode is for Transports that have moved or arrived via an ingress move this phase. Models making a Rapid Disembark need to follow the same rules the Transport had to follow when disembarking whilst also needing every model to be wholly within 3” of the Transport. Units that perform Rapid Disembarking can not charge in that turn.

Tactical Disembark: This mode is essentially “normal disembark;” it follows the normal Set Up 03.02 rules models are normally required to follow whilst again also needing every model to be wholly within 3” of the Transport. Units that use this mode can make normal and advance moves after disembarking, and there are no restrictions on their ability to charge.

Combat Disembark: This last mode lets you disembark into engagement range but only with units the Transport is engaged with, and it comes at the risk of losing models to hazard rolls. You're only forced to use this mode if there’s not enough space to disembark using the Tactical mode, which would allow your unit to move elsewhere or charge without risking the Hazard rolls.

Emergency Disembarking

If your unit is unlucky enough to be embarked inside a Transport that is destroyed, it is forced to make an Emergency Disembark move. Be aware that this rule has changed quite significantly in the app though! here's the full rule as of July 2026.

The first thing to note about this rule is that while the disembark distaince is 6", models using this disembark move must be set up as close to the Transport as possible. So if there's room for the model to be placed touching the transport it has to be placed there. This is why this all happens before the transport is removed.

If a TRANSPORT model is destroyed, before removing it from the battlefield, the active player must make an emergency disembark move (see opposite) with each unit embarked within it.

The added lines is pretty fundamental though, adding an escape clause for models that can't deploy following the the usual Set Up 03.02 rules.

OR: if the above is not possible while remaining unengaged, set up that model wholly within the set-up distance of that Transports, and as close as possible to that transport, and engaged.

Note that this clause is a "while moving" one, which means that you don't need to keep shifting models around looking for a configuration where none of them are engaged. Instead it's check that occurs each time you place a model. If the only position available where the model fits is one where it's engaged with an enemy unit you can place the model there.

Note on this though that the priority is to place models unengaged, if there are two positions available and one of them is closer to the transport but would result in the model being engaged you must put the model in the position that doesn't result in the model being engaged.

Assault and Shock Disembark Moves

August's update added two new Disembark Moves to the roster: Assault Disembark Moves and Shock Disembark moves! These two moves and their associated FAQ resolve an issue with the current Disembark Move that I didn’t even notice. If your model has an ability such as the Devilfish’s Rapid Deployment, it didn’t have a valid Disembark move type.

Rapid Deployment: Units can disembark from this TRANSPORT after it has Advanced. Units that do so count as having made a Normal move that phase, and cannot declare a charge in the same turn, but can otherwise act normally in the remainder of the turn.

Or the Land Raiders’ Assault Ramp ability.

Assault Ramp: Each time a unit disembarks from this model after it has made a Normal move, that unit is still eligible to declare a charge this turn.

This also did not previously have a valid Disembark Move type to choose other than Combat Disembark; Rapid Disembark required the transport to have made a normal or ingress move, while Tactical Disembark required a transport to have remained stationary, meaning these abilities required you to make hazard rolls and the unit became battle-shocked. That's something the new Disembark Moves show was clearly not intended.

There is however one small issue with the new moves that I hope is addressed quickly in the app:

The new Shock Disembark’s after moving section doesn’t really seem to make sense; in fact it appears to be the wording added to the Consolidation rules for Ongoing Consolidations (see above). I strongly suspect that this section should actually read:

"AFTER MOVING: Until the end of the turn your unit is not eligible to declare a charge."

As of right now, that section doesn’t make much sense; a unit embarked within a transport can’t start their Disembark Move engaged with anything, as it’s not on the battlefield. Fortunately the abilities themselves do preclude making a charge, so we can be pretty confident on the RAI here.

Q&A

Can a disembarking model be hidden?

Yes. For a model to be hidden it needs to be INFANTRY/BEAST/SWARM, be within terrain a terrain area that contains one or more light/dense terrain features, and not have made any ranged attacks during this turn or the previous turn. So if your transport was for instance destroyed by an enemy attack and the unit inside makes an emergency disembark move, then it’s possible for them to finish that move in a position where the unit would benefit from the hidden rule.

How does disembarking large models work?

The rules for how disembarking works for larger models are in a slightly odd place in the Warhammer 40k App. Rather than cover it with the Transport rules, it’s covered in Set Up 03.02 as part of Setting Up Large Models 03.02.02.

Disembarking from a Transport: When a unit disembarks from a TRANSPORT, it must be set up wholly within 3" of that model. If a disembarking model is so large that it is not possible to set it up wholly within 3" (typically because it is itself larger than 3" in all directions), set that model up with its base within 1" of that TRANSPORT’s base (or hull), and not engaged with any enemy units.

The main difference here is that instead of the model needing to be wholly within 3”, it now needs to be within 1”.

That's all for this weeks Ruleshammer; if you have some questions you think I should cover in the future though please do send them via this form!  Have any other questions or feedback? Thoughts

Sneaky mid-weight tunnel bugs face off against a very grindy Leagues of Votann build, which still takes Reconnaissance despite being fairly light on fast stuff.

The challenge for the Tyranids here is that the Votann have no particular incentive not to be aggressive, and likely win a knock-down confrontation. The bugs don't really have the concentrated threats available to take down some of what the Votann are packing, and the Land Forts are a particular problem - only the Hive Guard really scratch them, and as soon as the Votann make it to Fortity, that stops being true because Void Hardened will be available. As the Votann, you want to prioritise making that happen, then send forward in force, trusting on your might to take the Tyranids out of the game.

With that in mind, the Tyranids need to try and front load their scoring as much as possible, which on this mission is at least somewhat plausible, especially if they accompany it with some good, old fashioned move blocking using the Hormagaunts. I think end-game scoring is just fully out for the Tyranids, so they need to deploy for going first - prepare the Leapers to go Action on a far objective to bank 4/4/2 on Primary turn one, then clinging onto their expansion for dear life, aiming to physically stop the Votann reaching it by any means necessary, and sustaining 10VP turns (4 for holding one, 4/2 for decoys). I think they're really hoping for layout A here, but if the standard ABCAB pattern was followed, then sadly they get the Dawn of War map, which is kind of the worst for them. The only route for them is that maybe if they can judiciously pick off enough enemy units, they can stop the Votann having enough pieces to contest a wide front (especially against tunnelers), as they're a bit lower on activations.

I do also like how clutch the biovore is here - for this mission specifically, a 6"  bubble of "can't end an Advance" is exceptionally good, as it can protect a key decoy token from getting cleared. I do think the Tyranids probably get ground down, but they have enough tools to make the Votann fight for it, and delaying them does present a path to victory. A valiant attempt seems to have been made on that front, but not quite enough to stop the Leagues taking the prize.

title: Warmachine's latest model reveal is proof that cartoony minis can still be totally badass
content:
On Tuesday, steampunk fantasy wargame Warmachine revealed an absolute unit of a unit. 'Dozer and Smigg, Siege Breakers', are a little and large pair consisting of a huge troll so heavily armored he's practically a walking castle, and a Pygmy troll brave enough to ride on his back and operate a double-barrelled siege cannon. It's a miniature that's as silly as a cartoon and as cool as a cucumber, and a great reminder that models don't have to be grimdark to look awesome.

Dozer and Smigg are actually returning characters, who had a pretty big miniatures in the previous edition of Warmachine, but their new version fits onto a hefty 80mm base. Publisher Steamforged Games has revealed some of their rules; they're a mobile artillery unit for the Southern Kriels Kithguard, who support their ambushing allies by firing on nearby enemy troops whenever another troll unit emerges from a tunnel.

They're big and uncomplicated and I love them. They're also the furthest thing from my usual tastes in miniature wargames - grimdark and gothic minis, particularly Warhammer 40k and Trench Crusade - you can get. They're just not that serious. And that got me thinking about how fantasy wargame aesthetics have evolved during my lifetime, because "serious" miniatures are relatively recent.

The famous 'heroic' miniature style that Citadel Miniatures pioneered in the 80s and 90s - with big hands and heads - evolved in response to constraints, the limits of what it was possible to sculpt by hand, and what you could feasibly cast in metal in a two-part rubber mold. It was exaggerated, and therefore kind of cartoony.

Those limits don't apply any more. Games Workshop uses 3D design to make extremely detailed kits that break big 3D shapes into pieces that fit together perfectly, and it takes advantage of lightweight plastic to create top-heavy models, often with large empty volumes. It hasn't become realistic, but it has become less cartoony, and - outside the Orks - a lot more sober.

The Warmachine line was designed around the limitations of metal model production in the early 2000s - in fact it revelled in those constraints, celebrating the fact that every Warjack model was a half pound of solid white metal. The world that they existed in was big and heroic and just a little bit cartoony, with plenty of comedy characters (from Gobbers to Gremlins) alongside the more serious warriors and Warcasters, and plotlines that were as much comic book heroism as they were fantasy epic.

Today the model range is almost entirely 3D printed with a tiny number of plastic kits, but instead of adapting the design style in response to the old constraints being lifted, its taken that classic style beyond what was actually possible in metal (or economical in cold-cast resin). Dozer and Smigg are a perfect example of this - traditionally casting them would be feasible, but it would also be miserable - yet they're a definite continuation of that classic style.

A more direct comparison would be the updated Menoth range. The religious fundamentalists of Menoth haven't evolved technologically in years, and the new model kits represent very similar machines to those they fielded in the previous edition of the game. They're extremely close to the older designs, but with the material costs and physical weight of the minis lower, they're bigger and bolder than before - a realization of a full metal fantasy with non-metal materials.

All of this to say, I like these minis. With the near unlimited freedom of 3D sculpting and 3D printing, it's great to see design traditions that have their roots in older production methods explored well beyond what was once conceivable.

What do you think? What's your favorite miniature sculpting style, and why? Let me know in the Wargamer Discord community!
